Two temples cut into a sandstone cliff above the Nile at Abu Simbel, in the far south of Egypt near the border with Sudan, built for Ramesses II around 1264 to 1244 BCE. Four seated statues of the king, each about 20 metres tall, guard the front of the Great Temple.

The site was a message to Nubia, the land to the south, about Egyptian power. The Great Temple honours three great gods and Ramesses himself as a god. Twice a year, in February and October, the rising sun shines through the whole temple onto the statues in the inner room. The smaller temple honours his queen Nefertari and the goddess Hathor.

Sand buried the temples for centuries until European travellers found them in 1813. In the 1960s the Aswan High Dam, built under Gamal Abdel Nasser, was about to drown them under Lake Nasser. A campaign led by UNESCO cut both temples into more than a thousand blocks and rebuilt them on higher ground. The rescue helped launch the idea of World Heritage Sites.
